utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case Number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin and Daryl Mundis, assisted today by our intern, Lisa Hartog, and our case manager, Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, and Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On the 1st of March, 2005, the 188th day of sitting, we bid good morning to the witness, the professor, the representatives of the Prosecution, all the Defence attorneys, the accused, General Hadzihasanovic, General Kubura, and I bid good morning also to all the personnel of this courtroom who are assisting us and all those outside the courtroom. Before giving the floor to the Prosecution who will begin the cross-examination, I should like to ask the Defence about the documents. In the expert report in the footnotes, a series of documents are mentioned. However, in the summary table that you have provided there's again a whole series of documents. For example, the first document in the list, 350, is the constitution of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You provided yesterday a small binder, but in that small binder I did not find the documents mentioned in the footnotes, nor the documents in -- on this list. What do you intend to do subsequently regarding these documents? At what point to you wish to tender them? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Madam Judge, good morning, Your Honour. All these documents are part of three binders which have already been provided to the Prosecution some time ago for them to be able to prepare for the testimony of the expert. All these documents except the two or three that I mentioned yesterday are documents appearing on the list of Defence exhibits, and once the testimony of the expert has been completed we intend to ask for the admission of these documents into evidence. As for the footnotes, you will notice that the majority of the documents mentioned have already been admitted into evidence because they are DH exhibit whereas others have a number. The footnote on page 3 refers to document 19 -- no, no, a footnote on page 2 refers to a document that is called 1629, Defence Exhibit 1629. This is a new document and we will ask to tender this document into evidence as soon as the testimony of the professor has been completed. If the Chamber wishes to have copies of these documents to put questions to the witness, we do have copies that we can provide. The witness has copies and the Prosecution and each of those documents had been pressed on the ELMO during the testimony of this witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon, for this explanation. Our understanding is that at the end of the hearing you will be asking to tender the documents mentioned in the footnotes as well as those on the list of documents which were disclosed to the Prosecution, and I have the numbers from 350, the last one being 465. I shall now give the floor to Madam Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours, good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Ms. Henry-Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Trnka, good morning. My name is Tecla Henry-Benjamin, and along with me is my colleague Mr. Daryl Mundis, assisted by our case manager and intern, and we represent the Prosecution. Your examination-in-chief yesterday was very detailed and strictly to the point with respect to the expert report for which you are here today and for which was tendered in evidence. And as such I have a few questions with respect to clarification on what you said yesterday. If at any time during the examination you do not understand what I'm saying or you wish me to rephrase the question for any reason, feel free to do so and I will certainly oblige. Sir, my understanding is that you -- because of your qualifications and academic background and experience in the constitutional law you were requested to prepare an expert report for the Trial Chamber. But my further understanding is that you -- because of your non-academic background and lack of experience in military law and criminal law you do not qualify or see yourself as an expert in these two disciplines of the law. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Your Honour, Mr. President, Your Honours, Madam Benjamin, good morning. Thank you for your question. I said yesterday that I do have a degree in law but my specialty is constitutional law. So I delved deeper into the problems of criminal responsibility and regulations within criminal law, and I also consulted regulations linked to internal relations and responsibilities in the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for this purpose. I think that my general knowledge in law and legal qualifications do allow me to give an opinion about these matters, though I of course prefer constitutional law. In any event, principles of criminal law in most democratic systems are a part of constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. And I ask you the question to say this or to inquire from you that any opinion offered in the two areas, i.e., criminal law and military law, would be limited to the interpretations of the regulations on the law as you see fit and not as an expert. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are not. I don't know what you mean by inclination. I am speaking from the point of view of theory and practice of constitutional law and the elements of constitutional law that are applied in criminal law and the law in the armed forces, in this case of the Yugoslav army. So I think I can speak about those relationships with some conviction, but of course it is up to the Court to decide whether I am right or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, you would not be able to assist the Trial Chamber specifically with the military commands and the chains of the military commands, would you?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't go into the details of the relationships within the army; that is not my immediate specialty. But the chain of command is actually what starts with the civilian control of the armed forces and, as we have shown in a number of charts, we see a clear vertical line going from the Presidency to each individual commander at various levels. Of course certain purely military matters are those for which I do not consider myself competent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let us begin with the conflict itself. What would in your opinion be the overriding factor for the cause of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me, Madam Prosecutor, to remind you of my testimony yesterday in which I said that in order to understand the situation in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and therefore in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, one should bear in mind that there were two major processes that occurred within a short period of time and which are of great historical significance. You will remember that I mentioned the breakup of the former socialist or communist system of the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, a part of which was the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, as the name itself indicates, and secondly, the breakup of the country itself, at first into four plus one entities; that is, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Macedonia on the one hand, and Serbia and Montenegro on the other. The breakup of a country of this kind should be seen within the context of the events in the former Yugoslavia and particularly the year 1974 when there was greater emphasis on the independence and statehood of the republics. Also one should bear in mind various concepts that were at play in the territory of former Yugoslavia, and the nationalist forces -- and here I wish to stress the difference between national and nationalist, because national indicates the assertion of cultural, linguistic, and other characteristic of an ethnic group, whereas nationalism actually means the abuse of national feelings and affiliation with a particular ethnic group to achieve goals at the expense of other peoples and other individuals. That is why I wish to point out that already in the former Yugoslavia such nationalist aspirations were developing endeavouring to impose the concept of one -- a single nation state. There were attempts for the members of one ethnic group to live in one state. This is a purely nationalistic idea which has nothing in common with the democratic concept of a nation and a civil state, but it was of great relevance in the period of the breakup of the former Yugoslavia. The protagonists of this idea felt that this international context as well as the domestic context provided a chance for the fulfilment of those nationalist aspirations. One should not forget that most of the members of the Serb people were living and still live in the Republic of Serbia, whereas a certain portion were in Bosnia and Herzegovina, about 32.3 per cent of the population were of Serb ethnicity in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And also, the vast majority of the Croatian population lives in the Republic of Croatia and 17.6 per cent of the population of Bosnia and Herzegovina are of Croat ethnicity. And these mother national states, if I can call them that, and the nationalist ideologies and their leaders and protagonists felt that this was an opportunity to motivate their compatriots in Bosnia and Herzegovina to fulfil the idea that I mentioned a moment ago. If one has in mind the fact that in the former Yugoslavia, as I said yesterday, the military structure was highly centralised and the single party that was in power was also centralised with a certain degree of autonomy reflected in the existence of central committees in the republics, but the principle of democratic centralism applied and therefore decisions had to be implemented from the top down. In the meantime and due to other circumstances that we don't have time to go into, the ethnic composition of the command personnel of the former Yugoslav army was dominated increasingly by Serbs. The regime in Belgrade in power at the time counted on this, and I think that these two elements provide the main causes of the conflict that broke out in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. However, one should not bear in mind that with the collapse of the communist system factors of stabilisation could be provided by elements of a civic society, which unfortunately had still not been constituted. And I indicated yesterday some of the key changes that occurred in 1990 and which were meant to lay the foundations of a civic democracy, but this was still far from being achieved. And through human rights this would have had an integrating effect throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia as we see in other democratic states. I hope I have managed in very brief lines to give you an answer. Of course I am at your disposal for any further clarifications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and you were indeed. Would you say that the failure of the plans, the Vance-Owen Plan, intensified the conflict?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can say with certainty that that is so; in fact, support this. The failure of both the Vance-Owen and the Vance-Stoltenberg Plan intensified the military conflict. The political situation was totally unclear. No other solutions were in the offing, and the armed forces were endeavouring to gain control of as much territory as possible so as to have a better position for any further negotiations. I pointed out in my expert report that unfortunately this national component was given priority, and there was always reference to provinces with a majority population. And the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan favoured the ethnic principle and proposed the formation of three national republics. It is quite clear in view of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina where the population in the ethnic sense is intermingled throughout the territory, the formation of such small ethnic statelets would actually encourage endeavours for the majority population to get rid of the minorities. Of course this would lead to greater intensity of conflict and that is what happened. In fact, the basis of the peace plan for Bosnia and Herzegovina which was eventually adopted was the Washington Agreement, which is not included in the time period covered by this case, when in 1994 the federation as a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina is no longer described as a country composed of ethnic cantons. On the contrary, ten equal cantons constitute the federation, and not one of them can have any ethnic characteristics nor may the name have any ethnic implications. With the introduction of the body of human rights corresponding to higher standards, in my opinion this created the preconditions conducive to a final peace settlement, which in fact happened in December 1995 when the war ended and peace was established through the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, could you state why in your opinion the Washington Agreement was such a good thing for Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say it was good. It provided only a partial solution to the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Surely you have noticed a provision of the constitution of the federation and of the Washington Agreement, which stipulates that the federation is formed on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina where the majority of the population are Bosniaks and Croats, whereas for the rest of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina solutions would be sought in the future, or words to that effect. So this was laying the foundations for the future order. And if I go further you will see that the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina which is part of the peace agreement of 1995 which stipulates that Bosnia and Herzegovina is a state in which there are three equal constituent nations and in which the rights of all other peoples and citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina are guaranteed. As a consequence of this provision, all exclusive national characteristics of entities are excluded. So the federation could not be called as some people called it the Croat-Bosniak federation, which has no basis in the Washington Agreement and especially not in the constitution, nor can Republika Srpska be considered an exclusive entity of one ethnic group. Because, as you probably know, the constitutional court provided additional interpretation of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, saying that both entities have to be formed in such a way that the equality of all ethnic groups and other citizens should be guaranteed in both. Let us recall Annex 7 which refers to the return of refugees and displaced persons, reflected efforts to eliminate the results of ethnic cleansing and to try without any illusions of being able to do everything, to try to reconstruct the ethnic composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, such as it existed according to the 1991 census. We are now witnesses of that process, and I am mentioning it only for you to understand the tendencies and the key reasons for those let us call them successful peace agreements, though I as a theoretician but also someone practicing constitutional law could find many shortcomings in both the Washington Agreement and the Dayton Accord.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your report you discuss the complexities of the functioning of the civilian authority and the military authority during wartime. And particularly, in paragraph 124 of your report at page 50 you said that: "Because of conditions of a state of war there are inherent complexities in the establishment and function of civilian authority and also to the structure of the ABiH, specifically the 3rd Corps." Professor, could you explain this perhaps by way of an illustration or example?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you can remember yesterday when I used a chart to show the structure, the way in which the military and civilian authorities functioned in, for example, Travnik municipality, you may have noticed that in that very small area there were military structures that functioned. There were the civilian authorities, and in parallel to the civilian authorities that had territorial jurisdiction there was a very developed structure of so-called displaced organs that were present there. So, for example, in the entire area of Banja Luka, this area had direct contact, personal contact, with the citizens who had fled from the combat and had arrived in territory of Travnik municipality, or rather in the territory of Central Bosnia. Bodies of power were formed there. And if you remember, we mentioned the entire structure of the civilian and military organisation of the HVO. If you bear in mind the fact that together with these bodies of power there were religious communities that have been displaced and that were in function and that there were certain -- or various social organisations, international organisations, that were also functioning, you will realise the complexity of the situation within a context of incessant fighting, within the context of various conflicts. So without a doubt, this shows how delicate the situation for the civilian and military authorities was. We must also bear in mind that at the time of the conflict of the ABiH and the HVO there were no points, no common points between these institutions. The HVO and the ABiH, if we take them outside and plan as an example, were supposed to act jointly in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but this was not the case. Institutions continued to be split, and the army had control over some of them and the HVO control over of others. And the army of the Bosnian Serbs was incessantly active as far as I know through the media on Vlasic and elsewhere because they were in the immediate vicinity. So altogether, this points to the fact that the situation was extremely delicate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I were to say that at all times during the conflict, and particularly in the period of the indictment that we are speaking about, that there was cooperation between the civilian and military structures at all levels? Would you agree that there was cooperation between the two bodies?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I have to be precise when answering your question as to whether there was such cooperation or not, referring to factual situation. I'm testifying as an expert on the system, and I'm testifying about how things should have functioned according to the system. Yesterday I tried to explain the vertical structure within the civilian authorities and the vertical structure within the military authorities. The system made it possible for there to be mutual cooperation at certain levels. Let's bear in mind the position of the security services centres for the Territorial Defence staffs at regional and local level. And it was their duty to provide information to the local authorities on matters of their responsibility, but they could not receive orders. The idea that such organs should be engaged was something that had to be authorised to the central authorities in Sarajevo. And if the centre in Sarajevo accepted such proposal, then through its chain of command or in another way it would forward the relevant information to the local organs, forward authorisation to the local organs. So I have no records, according to which this took place everywhere. You would really need to have the relevant material to be able to express a precise opinion on the matter. I am testifying about the way in which the system functioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with respect to the way in which the system functions, certainly in peacetime it functioned much differently than in wartime?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally. And this is something that we discussed yesterday and it's something that I have discussed at length in my report. Throughout the world when a state finds itself in exceptional circumstances, when there is a war. Because you know there is a theoretical difference between emergencies situations and imminent threat of war and a state of war. When a state, a society, finds itself in such a situation then the entire society, the entire state, restructures itself in order to mobilise all the men and all the resources for the defence of the country which is its primary task at such a point in time. We also mentioned what happened to the civilian authorities in such cases and above all what would happen to the parliaments which weren't adapted for wartime conditions. And the executive authorities in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina were in the hands of the Presidency in an enlarged formation, and it would take important decisions and have the possibility of amending the constitution, and this is that the Presidency did on a number of occasions in the course of the war. So, objectively speaking, the situation is different when the authorities have to operate in wartime and when they have to operate in peacetime. We should also add that communications with the central institutions of power are more difficult and often interrupted, and this means that within such a system it was necessary to take into account the possibility of such situations. As a result, sometimes -- I have already provided you with an example concerning the minister of justice, my predecessor, who authorised the regional organs to issue certain regulations so -- which the Ministry of Justice of Bosnia and Herzegovina would usually have issued. Naturally he asked them to confer with him about the document beforehand and to provide information on adopting it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. But the real and territorial jurisdiction of the judicial authorities was also adapted, amended. There were displaced institutions within the region of Banja Luka, and this is not something that would usually happen. You wouldn't have a court of the Banja Luka region or a military court of the Banja Luka region or a regular court which operated in Travnik. So the limits were also moved in -- as far as the real jurisdiction of courts were concerned. Sometimes the lower courts were authorised to deal with matters that higher courts would usually deal with. But these were wartime conditions and all the legal documents that were adopted in exceptional circumstances were subsequently to be ratified. And one attempted to make the wartime situation more regular and more in line with the sort of situation that would have prevailed in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a follow-up to what you've just said, isn't it a fact that during wartime that all armies, not only the ABiH, operated under or operate under extremely difficult situations? Isn't that common to all armies during wartime?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without a doubt there is certain restrictions, certain limits, that are a result of the situation. But I think that this shows the extent to which the authorities attempt to preserve a legal system in such exceptional circumstances. I believe that this is a very important element when assessing whether someone gave up applying legal provisions in wartime because the circumstances were exceptional. I think that if there are exceptional circumstances and one attempts to implement the regulations that must be implemented, this is positive. Yesterday I said - and this is in the report - I said that as far as the special military courts are concerned, you don't have such courts in peacetime. But given a wartime situation, it is not possible to tolerate certain excesses, incidents or excesses carried out against troops. But I think most armies throughout the world do provide for the possibility of such an institution in wartime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. As an expert and also being in the position yourself as Minister of Justice, can you explain or elaborate on the role the government played in the war, in particular the conflict in 1992 in conjunction with the army.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the government is concerned and its relation to the army, the government in fact had no influence on the army. If we don't take into consideration the fact that the Ministry of Justice is also part of the -- the Ministry of Defence is also part of the government. This is something that I have addressed in my report at greater length, but the civilian command structure from the Presidency went through the Ministry of Defence. But at that point it would branch off in two directions. Most of the duties that concerned the military went through the supreme command staff by this vertical line I have mentioned. If it was necessary to support military actions, this should be done through the Minister of Defence who embodied the civilian role in relation to the army. We should remember they had the responsibilities such as mobilisation, keeping military records, training, taking care of the population, et cetera, and this did not involve direct military engagement. In the report I believe that you have noticed that when I mentioned the responsibilities of the Presidency, its responsibilities controlled the armed forces, then these ten items were the responsibility of the Presidency alone. But the item that states that are other matters that the Presidency is responsible for when it comes to civilian commanding, it is also stated that the Presidency can render a special decision and to make the Minister of Defence responsible for certain issues. So the Minister of Defence is member of the government but within the ministry he mostly deals with the civilian issues. So there is something else one should bear in mind. The government had a fairly close relation, and this relation was important, a close relation with the civilian protection staff. The government then had the possibility of intervening in the affairs of the civilian organs and the local organs of power. They could prevent them from carrying out certain -- or implementing certain documents. They could ask for the constitutional court to render a decision on whether a certain act -- certain documents were in accordance with the constitution. And as far as other documents are concerned, there could be replacements. And I said that given that the order had been disturbed at the regional level, it was even possible for them to appoint a commission of their own who would be responsible for matters in a given region. So the government was mainly involved in implementing Presidency documents in wartime conditions because the Presidency functioned as the assembly, and these were documents that related to the organisation and functioning of civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday in elaborating on the report, you indicated that there could -- there is a possibility or there could have been a possibility that at the lower level the cases -- of cases where the civilian organs interfered in the jurisdiction of the military units. And I believe you said included the AOR of the 3rd Corps and it's in the report as well. Now, your function basically - and you keep repeating - is to inform the Trial Chamber as to what happens in principle, but certainly you couldn't tell us what happens in reality. So could you elaborate for me on this aspect for the sake of clarification because why would you say that there were cases where the local civilian organs were found interfering in the jurisdiction of the military units, because that is not what would have happened in principle, if I understand you?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll go back to my approach to the entire report. I've been testifying about the system in place for both sides, but given the documents that were placed at my disposal I came across a few rare cases in those documents. This doesn't mean that I know what the situation in the field was, but I came across some documents that showed that in exceptional -- in rare circumstances, the civilian organs would interfere with the jurisdiction of the military authorities. I also came across a number of cases in which you could mention a sort of borderline relation between the civilian and military authorities. I mentioned the documents I had in mind; I referred to them at the end of my report. In such cases, there was a clear distinction made between the area for which the military and the civilian authorities were responsible. Let's remember the authority of the civilian and military police and joint orders for joint action in the field, and it was clearly stated or the duties of each force were clearly stated. I also mentioned on the basis of what I had before me that there were cases in which the Executive Board of the Bugojno municipality issued, and I'd call them, instructions of some kind to the misdemeanours court, instructions with regard to penalties and a request was made for more severe penalties; and on the other hand, they even brought into question some of the acts of the court. For example, confirmation of contracts that the courts had carried out. And the organ of the civilian local authorities made -- requested that these contracts not be approved, requested that they be controlled by the organs of the executive power. So these are certain cases. I don't have any other records before me, and in order to assess this issue it would be necessary to review voluminous material that concerned the military and the civilian authorities. I think I have tried to explain how this system functioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I understand, and I think I did, it means that you deviated a little bit from your task, you went more into the factual approach there than into principle. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not correct when you say that I went more into the factual approach. I was far more concerned with the way the things functioned in the system. But I mentioned these individual cases to show whether there were cases in which the constitutional system was respected or whether there were any violations of this system. I never wanted to adopt the position of a factual witness. I mentioned these cases because they illustrate an assessment I made in my report. Perhaps one could have said that in certain cases the system or the order that was in place was not always respected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you have come across the reverse when perusing documents? Would you have come across where the ABiH 3rd Corps would have done the reverse?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't come across anything that would confirm such a -- the existence of such a situation. I believe that in one document, but I don't think it was a 3rd Corps document, perhaps it was from the Main Staff, I remember one document that says that the organs of internal affairs should be more involved in fighting crime. I didn't quote that because I think that that would have involved a conclusion rather than an order because the entire sentence doesn't indicate that it's an order or an attempt to establish a relation of subordination. Naturally, we should bear in mind the fact that when the Presidency itself decides that the armed police force should be involved in army tasks, then the army has a legitimate authority of such a police contingent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks, Professor. Professor, I believe you would agree with me when I say that in theory or in principle there might not have been any influence, but what happens in practice could be an entirely different affair. And could you assist us, if it's possible, as to the other side of the coin, as to if there's a possibility that the principle could not be adhered to in wartimes, for whatever reasons.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately I didn't come across any such document. No such document was placed at my disposal. I can't claim that this never occurred; I really don't know. But on the basis of what I had before me, I didn't come across any examples of such traumatic interference, apart from the fact that I have -- apart from the case that I just mentioned. I never came across such examples. So I have the impression that the civilian authorities, in spite of all the difficulties they encountered, maintained their position, the position they had according to the -- in the constitution and they acted legally. I never had the impression that the army tried to take over control of the territory, whereas the civilian authorities should have had such control. I didn't have the impression that the military tried to carry out some sort of a coup d'etat or take over control of the entire territory. That wouldn't have been in accordance with the constitutional order. You must bear in mind that while the authorities were in power, and especially during the period that the relevant to this case, the war in our country was very well-documented, I would say. Many international institutions monitored the war. There were the European Monitors, there was the institute for the protection of human rights, et cetera. And in this case and in other cases, I didn't gain the impression that any of these international monitors mentioned would have referred to -- since I was involved in those negotiations as part of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina team, I was responsible for constitutional affairs. As such, I wanted the situation to be clear with regard to the -- I wanted the situation to be clear for the international community. I wanted them to realise that the army wasn't trying to influence the civilian authorities. If a commander had tried to exert such an influence and if I had any documents about this, I would have certainly interpreted the document in an adequate way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, at no time at all did it occur to you or did you feel that you should have done research on the other side as well to complete the whole picture, to compare and contrast what happens in principle in peacetime and what happens in principle in wartime so as to give a complete picture. Don't you think that something is missing so that we could get -- or so that history would have been afforded the privilege of seeing the whole picture?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assignment, according to the request of the Defence, was to write a report on the functioning of the system, how it was designed and how it was implemented. Now, whether all the elements and activities at all levels differed would require enormous -- an enormous amount of research for me to draw any conclusions. But in the opposite sense, too, when civilian authorities influence military structures, I don't have any records of that. I mentioned only three cases that I had at hand. It was not my understanding that I was expected to go to the very end, but I agree with you that for a complete report for a very serious research project, to see whether it -- everything functioned like that in each and every detail, I assume through other witnesses and other documents you will be able to gain some insight there, but I did not understand that that was my assignment. My assignment was, in my understanding, a description of the system of authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole, and that is why the report is mostly devoted to this general issue and then also its application in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. And when you look at the document as such, you will see that the latter part is quite small. First of all, I didn't have the necessary documents; and secondly, it was not my understanding that I was expected to go into that matter in such great detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I have to agree with you that I did observe that what I thought was the most important aspect was indeed very small, and hence my limitations here. I wish to touch on the area of the districts, and I would like you to elaborate for us. How did the division of districts impact on the 3rd Corps operation?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have spoken of the reasons behind the formation of the district. And we see that the structure of the districts overlapped with the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. I mentioned this in my report. In the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps there were 24 municipalities, and 12 of those or half of the total were de facto under the control of Republika Srpska and the army of the Bosnian Serbs. Out of the remaining 12, most were fully de facto controlled by the Croatian Defence Council. True in a certain number of municipalities - and you can see this in the report - there was exclusive control of the army. And there were also some municipalities in which both the army and the HVO were active, which of course means that the 3rd Corps was operating under rather complicated conditions. Also from the standpoint of cooperation with the civilian authorities when that was necessary, because they had to confront an area under the occupation of the Bosnian Serbs, a part under the HVO, and a third part with shared jurisdiction, which was further complicated when the conflict broke out between the BH army and the HVO. So that the structure of the districts, in my opinion, did have some impact, especially as at the beginning. There was seven districts and later they were re-organised to form ten, so that some municipalities from other districts like Kupres and some others came within the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. So the structure of the civilian authorities and the territorial organisation of the army did not coincide, and I assume that this was a cause of difficulty for the people in charge of military units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But won't this be the same for all the armies in all the areas? Isn't this not anything specific to the 3rd Corps? Each individual army would have had their own complications. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say either way. I'm not familiar with the situation with other armies, but as I was working on this expert report regarding the constitution of Republika Srpska, the area in which the Army of Republika Srpska was active you had a rather simple civilian structure: Organs of Republika Srpska and municipal organs that were active in that area. And as a rule - and I didn't find this in their material - they did not have those dislocated institutions. So that with a great deal of reservation with respect to other armies, in view of all the complications I have referred to, I could not take this into account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did say in the report and in that area that basically they -- the system was functioning relatively well for wartime, that there was that communication between civilian authorities and military and that basically, except for few exceptions, blockades, things like that, basically things were progressing as should have been in principle. So how do you reconcile, you know, the difference?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to bear in mind all the circumstances that complicate the situation. And if you bear in mind all the difficulties the authorities had to grapple with, and if you take into consideration the regulations which allow for more flexible positioning of the authorities with changes in the factual territorial jurisdiction, the possibility for the Presidency to appoint presidents of municipalities that were not able to function properly, there were certain palliative measures taken for wartime, which insisted in maintaining what I would call a stable legality of the functioning of the civilian authorities, with all the restrictions and using all the possibilities allowed. Of course under ideal conditions and for peacetime conditions, the system wasn't functioning; but for wartime conditions and in view of the adjustment of regulations by the competent body, in this case the enlarged Presidency, I think that my conclusion is in order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in my learned friend's examination yesterday he put to you certain scenarios with respect to prosecutions and indictments laid and so on by the command of the 3rd Corps. And in one of the scenarios he described that if a military -- if a soldier and a civilian had gone into a village and committed an offence, crime of some sort, which court would this soldier could be tried in or -- and your response was: It would have had to be the civil court because he was not in combat and he was with a civilian, and so it would have to be the civil court. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't quite correctly interpret the first part of the question because the question was: If a civilian and a soldier were to torch a house and the house is not a military facility and is unrelated to the conflict - and this is very important - in that case, according to regulations in force regarding the competencies of regular courts, if a soldier and a civilian are co-perpetrators of a criminal offence or are suspected of being -- and these are not cases that come under the jurisdiction of a military court. It's not a question of attack on the armed forces or any jeopardy to the constitutional order - therefore, these were not actions that had to do with the activity of the army - then naturally it is the civilian court that is competent. There's no doubt about that, only you had to interpret the question fully.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I certainly did not interpret it fully because I still don't understand, and I'm going to ask you this question so we could see if we could clarify it: Is it your evidence that the military can only discipline a soldier for offences that are committed in combat or military-related offences? Is that what you're saying to us?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying the following: A soldier may be disciplined by his commander by the military disciplinary court, by the military court, for the offences clearly stipulated for such cases. But I also said that if a soldier is acting as a civilian, let us say if a soldier commits a traffic offence, if it is a minor offence he will be called by the magistrate courts, or if it is a graver offence then to the criminal court. And look at the regulation on military courts or decree on military courts, which clearly specifies the jurisdiction of military courts. So in principle, these courts try military personnel except when in cooperation with a civilian they committed an offence which does not fall under the jurisdiction of a military court. I think that is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me see if I could create a scenario, and perhaps we could get it clarified. If a soldier not in combat has left his unit, has gone into a village and has looted, in your opinion who is the person, or which department is responsible for prosecuting that soldier?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you would first have to explain whether the looting was done within the context of military operations, for revenge or to provoke ethnic hatred or intolerance. In that case, one could expect it to go to a military court. But if he committed an ordinary criminal offence and set fire to a house that has nothing to do with the military operations, I think it would be quite appropriate for him to be tried by a regular court. If there are no implications linked to protected values, if it is ordinary crime that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if it's ordinary crime and I am in my uniform and I deviate from my unit and I -- instead of taking a truck full of milk to one place, I take it to another - I may be in my uniform, I may not be - the army -- it is your opinion the district military prosecutor does not have the right to prosecute such a soldier, a member of its army?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. If he was wearing a military uniform, by his external appearance he has identified himself as a member of the army. So the military prosecutor would first have to investigate whether he was acting in accordance with his military duties as a soldier, and I think such action by a soldier could seriously affect the relationships in the local community. And I think that the district court should protect values in the area. If the soldier took off his uniform and committed that offence in civilian clothes, then I think it is the regular court that is competent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to belabour the point, but I think there is something that speaks about morale of the army and things like that. And in light of that I'm going to ask you this: If a soldier by the choice of apparel that a soldier chooses to wear, is it your opinion that that determines which court has jurisdiction over this soldier, or is it the person, the office that he holds, that has the jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the position of the army and the morale of a member of the army and the armed forces is something that every army protects. Let me remind you that for such acts -- if a soldier were to commit a burglary, the punishment would be very harsh, including the death penalty. So the punitive policy was designed to strengthen the morale of the soldiers. Because if soldiers were to commit criminal offences then such an army would have no respect from the people, and it would have no chance of attracting to its ranks as many people as possible to fight for the same goals as that army. So I certainly do not agree that an individual by putting on or taking off his uniform could decide where he would be tried. That is out of the question. If we look at the jurisdiction of the military court, it is quite clear, and it is not linked to this formal question of apparel. To disclose military or state secrets, undermining the combat ability of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the army and various other stipulations listed are what are decisive for the jurisdiction of the court and not the apparel of the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then I think we are both in agreement when I say that the district military prosecutor and the district military courts are not only necessarily for offences committed by its soldiers in combat but also can deal with crimes committed by their soldiers generally. It does not limit -- the district military court is not limited to crimes committed during combat, and that is where I think --

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- according to the regulations I have described, the competence of the military court, in my report, association to undermine the constitutional order, this need not have anything to do with military operations, but in that case also the military court would intervene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. On the question of reports and where my learned friend indicated to you a scenario where reports should be recorded and where prosecution should be recorded, and your response was that it could be found in the civilian archives, it can be found in the military archives. And I -- my question to you is this: If the prosecution's -- if the charges were brought by the military prosecutor and dealt with at the military court, would that record be also in the civilian court?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said if it came to the military court, which means that the prosecutor on the basis of the elements in the case judged that it was within the jurisdiction of the military court, then there are no such records in the civilian courts, except should the following happen: If one of the parties appeal against the decision of the district military court, the whole file goes to the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that, you will admit, is a civilian court. So in that case, you would be right, vice versa. If when a military prosecutor receives a criminal report, comes to the conclusion that the case does not fall within the terms of reference of his own or the military court, then he would forward that criminal report to a civilian body, to the civilian court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In light of what you have just said, could you elaborate on -- for us on the process between the military court and the appeals court. Could you explain to us how that operates.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I can say that in my opinion and from the standpoint of the system, it is of exceptional importance that the second-instance proceedings were within the competence of the civilian courts of the highest level. This fact in itself means that the Supreme Court will balance out the practice and, if you will, the punitive policy also in the application of criminal substantive and procedural law in both civilian and military courts. I see this as providing guarantees that military courts would not act as a corpus separatum in relation to the whole system, but they would have to fit into the standards applicable to a regular civilian system. And I think it was a very important provision avoiding the formation of an independent separate military system of prosecution. I think this is very important. So that when the matter is reviewed at the Supreme Court -- of course if it is a military secret, this will be done in private session; if it is not a military or state secret, if the court decides to have a hearing, though it does so rarely, it either revises the judgement of the first-instance court. Or if there is not sufficient evidence, it returns the case into the regular court - in this case the military court - indicating which facts needed to be verified once again. I think this is very important, and I think it's a good thing that we have managed to refer to it once again, though I mention it in the report, that this is a key fact reflecting the equal implementation of the law in both civilian and military courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one more question before the break, Mr. President. I think if I understand you well, the military court is not the final court. The military court, if there's an appeal, branches out now to the civilian aspect, which is the Supreme Court. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. That is why I think this is very important. The military court is only the first-instance court and always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think this should be a convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is almost 10.30. We're going to have the so-called technical break for about 25 minutes, and we will resume the hearing at about five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I give the floor again to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, I just have a few questions for you and then I will be done, and it surrounds the district military court that we have been trying to clarify and to understand. Now, correct me if I'm wrong or tell me if you agree with me when I say that the district military courts have jurisdiction over all their soldiers until -- up and until such time as a soldier is demobilised or discharged?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in the regulations. That means that with regard to the jurisdiction over military courts, then yes. Soldiers held to account, and this includes all acts committed as members of the armed forces. But as I have already said, if a soldier is not in uniform and he commits an ordinary crime within a civilian context, then we're no longer talking about a member of the military, we're talking about a civilian who would be held to account elsewhere. But to make sure that everything is clear, in paragraph 99 of my report and in paragraph 100, I provided a breakdown of crimes and of the jurisdiction of military courts. And for such crimes, civilians would be held to account before such courts and members of the military in principle would be held to account before such courts. When a soldier commits a crime in civilian clothes, usually it's the military court that deals with the soldiers, that puts these members of the military on trial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to repeat the very last sentence: "When a soldier commits a crime in civilian clothes, usually it's the military court that deals with the soldiers, that puts these members of the military on trial." Well, I think you will agree with what we say now, that if the soldiers deviate from the combat area and they commit a crime, the military court has jurisdiction over them?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, things are as follows. One assumes that the military court is responsible for such an individual, the report will be filed with the military prosecutor. But if the military prosecutor having examined all the circumstances that the crime is -- doesn't fall within the jurisdiction of the military court, if he establishes that it's an ordinary crime, then he will forward the case to the regular prosecutor's office. But as a rule, soldiers are held to account before military courts; civilians held to account before such courts in the circumstances I have mentioned. A minute ago I was mentioning the reverse situation, when a soldier is held to account before a civilian court, and that concerns cases in which he is a co-perpetrator in a crime. But civilian courts are responsible for civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regardless of whether the soldier has on a uniform or not, and I agree with you. The other one I wanted to get clarified was in respect to deserters. Would you agree with me that the military court has jurisdiction over deserters as well? Just bear in mind as deserters they have not been discharged, neither have they been demobilised.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, you have just confirmed that although he is a deserter, he abandoned the ranks of the army on his own initiative. So -- that he is nevertheless a member of the member and as such it is the military court that would have jurisdiction over such an individual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if deserters were to commit offences, then it is expected of the military prosecutor to proceed with charges against him; that is expected, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more. The special military courts, they are responsible for all crimes that are committed by the soldiers, regardless of whether the soldiers are in combat or otherwise while they're out in the field?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to be more precise. The jurisdiction of special military courts is regulated in a particular manner, and such courts won't have jurisdiction for all crimes because these special courts, the purpose of these special courts, is to act when the acts are extremely dangerous, when the crimes are extremely dangerous, extremely important, and they are to proceed expeditiously. For example, if the military unit is at some distance and it's impossible for the regular military authorities to take over the entire case, then special military courts function. There are certain crimes for which special military courts are responsible, and these are crimes such as rebellion within the army, refusal to obey orders, and in such cases it's not possible to wait for the cases to be dealt with in a regular manner. These special courts can only hand down the death penalty. This shows that they're responsible for especially serious cases, but there is the right to appeal, to defence counsel, et cetera. As soon as this special court or such a special court decides not to hand down the death penalty, they have to forward the case to the regular authorities, and in such cases, the regular military prosecutor's office and the regular military court will continue to deal with the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, thank you very much. You have been quite helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this ends cross-examination. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now give the floor to Defence counsel for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning, Professor. Further to the questions which have been put to you by my colleague from the Prosecution, I just would like to clarify a few of the issues which were discussed. And the first one is I would like to come back again on this issue of courts and jurisdiction in order to provide further information to the Judges and to the Trial Chamber. My first question deals with page 43 of your report, but to be more precise it deals with paragraph 104 --

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 104. Now, paragraph 104, Professor, goes along with footnote 86, which deals with the decree law on service in the army of the republic. And I would just like to confirm with you that according to Article 64 to 71 of the decree law on service in the army, that the accountability of military servicemen is regulated by this decree, and that basically you have a system inside the army and you have a system outside of the army which is, as you explain in paragraph 104, accountability in accordance with the regulations regulating criminal offences or regulations regulating misdemeanours in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you confirm that there are two possibilities for a soldier to face proceedings for a violation, which is inside the army and outside of the army pursuant to the system in place.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have to repeat certain things, naturally. As far as accountability within the army is concerned, it's necessary to make a distinction between disciplinary accountability and criminal accountability. Disciplinary accountability also has two levels of social danger. If there is a minor offence, a minor violation of the rules of military service, according to the rules this is called a misdemeanour, in such cases it's the commander, the immediate commander, who must take certain disciplinary measures and hand down a sentence of up to 30 days in military prison. Then there's the military misdemeanour court which deals with slightly more serious misdemeanours, but they're still misdemeanours. The penalties are somewhat harsher, and there are two levels to the proceedings. The Ministry of Defence has an appeal court that hear appeals in such situations. As far as criminal offences are concerned, a while ago I discussed the entire matter with Madam Prosecutor, the matter concerning the jurisdiction of military courts. As a rule, a soldier will be held to account before a military court if he is a member of the ABiH. A member of the armed forces can naturally appear before a court as a civilian if he has committed a crime that has nothing to do with his membership of the army. If the crime is an ordinary crime, he will be held to account before such a court, like in any other system. But as a rule, a member of the military is held to account before a military court. We mentioned one exception, that concerns crimes that were co-perpetrated with a civilian, for which a civilian court, a civil court, is responsible. So this is the hierarchy of institutions. These are the proceedings that instituted for crimes committed by members of the military. And such crimes range from misdemeanours to criminal offences for which certain penalties are prescribed. And I would also like to point out something which was mentioned yesterday. In wartime, all the penalties are more severe because naturally the level of danger, the threat of social values is greater in wartime. According to the criminal law adopted from the former Yugoslavia, we have such a law in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in addition to harsher sentences, there is a list of certain specific crimes, and I mentioned eight additional measures that can be taken, measures that are additional to the penalty. So this outlines the issue of the responsibility of members of the military in a certain sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. If we look at the decree law on service in the armed forces where you find the provisions whereby a member of the military can be sentenced up to 60 days in prison, whether by his commander or by the military disciplinary court, these sentences can follow any of the breaches found in the rules of military discipline. Is that what you have just referred to when you speak about the jurisdiction inside the military?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the law on misdemeanours, I think that this concerns the violations of the rules within the army. With regard to criminal offences, it's the military court that is responsible for such matters. So there's a special military structure that is involved in dealing with these cases that concern members of the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I just happen to be looking at -- I'm trying to find here the decree law on service in the armed forces which I unfortunately just cannot find right now because it refers here to footnote in your report which is footnote 86. And for some reason, I cannot find out.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Official Gazette number 11 from the year 1992, that's the one. And number 12, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just need a minute to find the decree law in question. My footnote refers to another footnote. If you just bear with me for a few seconds, I'll be able to find the relevant document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the Chamber could assist you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document in question is DH440, Mr. President. I'll have to ask for the Chamber's assistance, Mr. President, to find DH440. It's in the binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could you find DH440, please. Here it is. We found the document and the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Professor, I would like you to look at this decree law on service in the army of the republic, and more specifically at the article which deals with the offences which can be committed. And my question is, Professor, that you in response to the last question, you mentioned that inside the military - and I would just look at what you mentioned - you said it's -- with regard to criminal offences -- sorry. What my question is, Professor - I would like to try and make it simple and I apologise for the time I'm wasting here with the Court - is simply that: Within the military, within the rules of the army, there are a number of offences which are listed in the regulations. And for -- I would simply like you to confirm whether for each of those violations which are in the rules of the military, that a soldier can be punished for up to 60 days in prison or detention, whether it is by his commanding officer or by the military disciplinary court.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally that depends on the particular situation, the particular case. If the danger, the threat, to the social order is minimal and if there are mitigating circumstances and the crime is listed in the decree that you are referring to, then yes naturally this is a situation that could occur. But if the threat posed to the social order was not that insignificant, if there was a significant social threat, then the entire case would have to be referred to the military prosecutor's office, or rather, to the regional military court to deal with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. Now, my question to you is: If a commanding officer does use his powers of punishment and sentences a soldier for one of the offences which is in the regulations, or whether this takes place by the military disciplinary court, where would we find the records for these punishments having been awarded to soldiers of the unit?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, since the disciplinary court, the second level disciplinary court is formed within the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if an appeal was filed, which was most often the case, well in such cases you will find the archives in the Ministry of Defence, in the disciplinary court or the appeal court within the Ministry of Defence. If not, then it could be found in the regional defence staff archives. I assume, although I'm not sure, that if there were such regional military staffs, all this would take place within the framework of the corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. I move on now to -- within your report where you mentioned, to make clear, and this is -- you find this at paragraph 99 of your report, where you say that: "District military courts were responsible for crimes committed by military personnel, and in some cases for crimes committed by civilians." And my colleague from the Prosecution confirmed that with you in detail. What my question relates to is the two exceptions to this rule, and the first being at paragraph 101 of your report that only in these cases would a member of the military would be tried by a civilian court other than the district military court.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something that I have mentioned on a number of occasions in paragraph 101. I'll quote the decree, the relevant decree, which states the following: "If a military serviceman and a civilian have committed a crime as co-perpetrators or as other accomplices and the trial of a civilian falls within the jurisdiction of a regular court, that court shall also try the military serviceman." That is found in article 9, paragraph 1 of the decree law on district military courts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, my question to you is: In such a case where this article applies and a soldier is tried before a civilian jurisdiction, if this -- can you confirm that this may take place either at the misdemeanour court, the municipal court, and the higher court?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this comes out in translation, but it's necessary to make a clear distinction. The misdemeanour court, because the civilians -- there is a municipal court for misdemeanours which has jurisdiction over civilians. But if we provide a strict legal interpretation of this provision, it concerns a criminal offence. A misdemeanour is not a criminal offence. It follows that such a combination occurs in the cases of criminal offences. However, this provision -- this is called a decree law on district military courts. It deals with military legislation. By analogy, one would probably draw the conclusion that when a soldier has committed a misdemeanour together with a civilian, then that member of the military would also be held to account for the misdemeanour. And usually these are traffic offences or disturbances of law and order. That's the essence of misdemeanours. If a soldier was in a car with a civilian and committed a traffic offence, drove through a red light, in such cases he'll probably be held to account. Perhaps it's not a good example because one of the individuals is driving the car and the other wasn't. But we could provide another example in which this analogy could be made. But to be more precise, it would be necessary to have a look at all the items of the provisions on military misdemeanours to see whether there is a relevant provision there. On the basis of legal logic, I come to the conclusion that the analogy would be appropriate here, but naturally to make analogies concerning criminal law is not really permissible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Professor, for the same in terms of criminal offences before either a municipal court or the higher court, then it would not be a matter of analogy but it would be that if a civilian -- pardon me, a member of the military who is in the situation covered by paragraph 101 of your report, and he is tried together with a civilian before a civilian court for a criminal offence, that this can take place before the municipal court and the higher court?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, but you must not forget a part of the wording which says if a civilian court is competent for that offence. This is a very important phrase. Because if the military court is competent for that particular act then both would be tried by a military court. So if you have a situation where the civilian court is responsible for the civilian, then the serviceman will also be held accountable by that court. If at the first instance, then it would be in the basic court, appealed to the higher court as appeals court; or if at the first instance it is within the competence of the higher court, then it will have to be appealed by the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. And just to confirm that, of course if a member of the military is tried before either the municipal court or the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. higher court, then the records of those proceedings will necessarily be in the municipal courts and in the higher courts?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or in the Supreme Court, if the appeals procedure took it as far as the Supreme Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'll move on to another area which was a question raised by my colleague. My colleague raised with you the issue of the Vance-Owen Plan as being a reason for the intensification of the conflict. What I would like to ask in respect of this issue is first of all: What was the attitude of the Presidency in respect of the Vance-Owen Plan? And more specifically, in respect of paragraph 6 of your report, the last sentence of which reads as follows: "It was clear that the existing national mixture could be eliminated only by violent means." So my question is: What was the attitude of the Presidency in respect of the Vance-Owen Plan and in respect of this conclusion of yours that the existing national mixture could be eliminated only by violent means?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina are concerned, upon certain suggestions they accepted the Vance-Owen Plan. And the president of the Presidency went to Athens, and I also travelled with him to Athens on the 2nd of May, 1993 when the Vance-Owen Plan was signed. So he had the support of the regular authorities. It should be noted, however, the Vance-Owen Plan did not strictly divide the provinces on the ethnic criterion because there were ten provinces envisaged, as can be seen from the annex attached to the report, so that it was possible to work out which ethnic group had the majority in each of those provinces. But the Vance-Owen Plan did not insist too much on this ethnic criterion and that is why it was more or less acceptable to the regular institutions of authority which consistently insisted that all the plans should not strictly divide up the three nations, but rather that it should ensure the equality of those nations on the basis of the concept of constituent nations which appeared in all the plans from the Cutileiro Plan to the Dayton Accords. But the Presidency and other organs of authority accepted this plan as it spoke of ten provinces and also envisaged special independent institutions for certain infrastructural facilities such as the railways, the power supply system, et cetera, which would be -- which would establish economic links throughout the whole territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is why the Vance-Owen Plan was objectively acceptable. But the question is: How individual forces within Bosnia and Herzegovina interpreted these ten provinces. And there was a special issue regarding the separation of military forces. And maybe there was a certain degree of inconsistency in that respect in the plan because the general principle was that military units with the background of one ethnic group would withdraw to the provinces in which that ethnic group dominated. So again, there was this concept of ethnicity. And this was a highly sensitive issue, especially in the provinces I mentioned, I think eight, nine, and ten, in which the Croats and the Bosniak population accounted for about 50/50 per cent. And when the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina was designed, this canton, which is known as the Central Bosnian canton based in Travnik, was provided with a special regime that differed from the other cantons in order to maintain the balance between Bosniaks and Croats. And if you look at the statistics about municipalities for the whole region of Central Bosnia, you will see that the percentage share between Bosniaks and Croats is more or less balanced, with the Serbs being present but in such smaller numbers. So this interpretation of this provisional provision, had the plan succeeded, it was a technical method of separation of armed forces, the aim being to create a factual situation which in the future might be in the interest of one or other military formation. I should like to recall that in fact the authorities of the Bosnian Serbs after formally signing the document later withdrew their signature and the Vance-Owen Plan failed. But precisely because it failed and because they saw that it was quite uncertain when a peace settlement would be found at all and what the components of that settlement would be, there was certainly attempts to gain factual control of as much territory as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'd like now to move to an issue which was raised by my colleague, and that is paragraph 124 of your report dealing with the complexity of the circumstances created by the war. And my question is as follows: Why did the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina insist on having displaced organs for the territories occupied, for example, by the VRS in Banja Luka? Why was it so important for the republic to have these displaced organs rather than simply not have any organs for occupied territory?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I answered that question to some extent yesterday. According to international war law, the force occupying a certain territory does not have the right to change the civilian structure of authorities. The army of the Bosnian Serbs, however, did not consider themselves to be an occupying army. But regardless of that, viewing things from the point of view of the legal authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they proceeded from the position that occupation, because the occupation was carried out by illegal military structures, that it was a temporary situation and that legally and factually it must not be recognised.
