For that particular reason, because occupation was treated as a temporary situation, organs of authority were formed, in fact one might say a complete structure of civilian and military authorities that were dislocated to territories under the control of the ABiH and those organs continued to function. So the first reason was one of principle, not to recognise the occupation; and the second reason is for these organs, too, to join in efforts to defend the country which meant that those organs were to exercise state authority with respect to citizens who as a result of the occupation under combat operations had either been expelled or had to fled to territory under the army's control, to work with those people just as the district authorities that were responsible for the territory. So the personnel responsibility also existed to keep records of able-bodied men, to give military training for them, and to do everything else for them to assist in the defence in the country, and that is why such dislocated bodies existed. Similarly, such institutions were established for non-governmental institutions, religious communities, social organisations, et cetera, and also of course there were international organisations, observer missions, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You mentioned in response to a question from my colleague the difficulties created by the organs having -- or the personal jurisdiction of the displaced organs and the territorial jurisdiction of the organs of the free territory. Now, my understanding on the basis of your answer is that of course neither the HVO nor the VRS or the Serb authorities had to deal with this concept of displaced organs. And I would like you to come back to how and what kind of practical problems this created for the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the free territories where they dealt with both types of jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I didn't quite understand the part of the question in which you mentioned the authorities of the Bosnian Serbs and the HVO. What does that have to do with the question you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will clarify my question, Professor. Maybe I can split the question in two; it will make it easier. The first question would be: Did the Serb authorities in the territory occupied by the Serbs and did the HVO in the territory under the power of the HVO have to deal with the concept of displaced organs?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now it's quite clear; I understand the question. Neither in theory nor in practice did they deal with that matter. It was of no interest to them. They were concerned with the situation in areas under their own control. Of course they were not enthusiastic about the fact that there was a Banja Luka district, a Doboj district, that such authorities existed, and they probably ignored those bodies because they felt that they were responsible for that territory. But that did not change anything because those organs did function, but under the circumstances that we have described they acted on a personal principle, and the Judges know full well that it is absolutely unusual in law, except in the case of certain organisations such as the church or some others, that this personal principle be applied. For the civilian authorities this is common knowledge, that the civilian authorities function on the territorial principle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now for this second part of this question. Given that the only party which had to deal with the concept of displaced organs, and of course the difficult situation created by the conflict between personal jurisdiction and territorial jurisdiction, that the only party who had these problems was the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the army of the republic, which was as you mention the only legitimate force and the only legitimately recognised government, what sort of practical problems would this cause in the working of the institutions?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me elaborate a little bit on the first part of the question. As the legitimate authorities and government elected in 1990 insisted on the respect of international law in the first place and respect of the fact that the state had been internationally recognised as a sovereign state and to preserve those attributes of a state, it acted in accordance with the standards of international law which meant not recognising occupation. And by not recognising the legitimacy of factual powers in that territory, it formed dislocated bodies whose legitimacy was derived from the elections and who aspired to establishing their territorial competence as soon as conditions allowed. And that was the motive why only the authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina insisted on this point. In a relatively small territory, though the percentages varied depending on combat operations, but even in the assessment of the Presidency at the beginning of the conflict, mention is made of 70 per cent of the territory being occupied. And if we add to this the very unclear situation at times between the ABiH and the HVO, then one can imagine how complicated the situation was to achieve on such a small territory with such a large population which lacked the elementary means of livelihood, accommodation in collective centres, improvised accommodation, they joined military units, et cetera, et cetera, and the territorial jurisdiction -- the authorities with territorial jurisdiction and those with personal jurisdiction had a great deal of difficulty under conditions of wartime and in view of difficulties in communicating with the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they had enormous problems without any doubt. And Madam Prosecutor drew attention to a very important point, and my position is - and I think that all the evidence speaks in favour - that in spite of all those circumstances the thread of legitimacy of the state authorities was preserved in spite of all those adverse circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. One last question on this specific issue. By reading your report, the section dealing with specifically the 3rd Corps, we get a clear picture that the commander of the 3rd Corps has a very large area of responsibility, most of which is occupied by the VRS and the Serb authorities, and a big part of what is left being under the control or power of the HVO. My question to you is: What kind of practical problems would this create for the commander of the 3rd Corps in dealing with the civilian institutions?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that neither the civilian nor the military authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had any influence over the part of the territory that was under occupation of the army of the Bosnian Serbs, and the population had moved to this side. It should also be noted that the HVO, and especially at the municipal level, was a specific combined military and civilian structure. One might even say that the HVO was a military force which also exercised civilian authority, which in my opinion differed significantly from what was happening in the territory under the control of the legal authorities. But if we now focus on the situation as it was in this very narrow area in which the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina were operating and also the military formations of BiH, this was clearly a source of great difficulty not only for the civilian authorities but also for the military component.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I move to another area which was covered by my colleague. A question was asked to you concerning the power of the enlarged Presidency, and you responded by saying that the enlarged Presidency in times of war had exceptional powers including the possibility to modify laws and even the constitution. Now, yesterday we covered already and you explained the need for these changes to be sort of ratified by the assembly when it would meet. But my question deals with the situation before the assembly has an opportunity to meet and ratify these decree laws and changes to the constitution. My question is: Could the constitutional court intervene if there was a decision made by the Presidency, by the enlarged Presidency, which was contrary to the constitution?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that from the standpoint of comparative constitutional law, all constitutional systems in the world stipulate the so-called extreme necessity. When the executive power, the president of the republic or the government or whatever the name of the executive may be, acquires considerable authorities in cases of war and in some constitutions in cases of other emergencies or extraordinary circumstances. So when it is noted or established that according to our constitution it was a state of imminent war or a state of war, then automatic procedures start functioning envisaged by the constitution when the executive authority acquires constitutional authorisation, which means legitimate authorisation. As the Presidency now passed a large number of decree laws, in French "decret loi," those decree laws were published in the Official Gazettes, indicating the day when they come into effect. So from then on they become a component part of the legal system. Being a component part of the legitimate legal system, they are subject to constitutional control as well as administrative control that I mentioned yesterday, but we're now focusing on constitutional control, and there were quite a number of cases when the constitutional court did intervene with respect to decrees passed by this enlarged Presidency and by its decisions quashed them and eliminated them from the legal system because they judged that they were not in accordance with the constitution. And I mentioned several such examples in my report, and this is further evidence that regular institutions of authority in spite of all difficulties did manage to exercise their functions as stipulated by the constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. One last question on this issue. You mentioned examples in your report. As paragraph 95 and in footnote 80 you discuss a decision which was taken on the dismissal of a judge or a judge juror which could be rendered even if the proceedings necessary to establish the dismissal would not have been conducted. And if I understand your report correctly, you mention that the constitutional court intervened and said that this was contrary with the BH constitution and this specific decree law was declared unconstitutional. Can you provide further information on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may interrupt. I do not think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: -- in any way in cross-examination was this raised, neither was it raised in examination-in-chief. So I do not know, you know, if my friend should be allowed to go that route. The report is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Benjamin is objecting. You're addressing the problem of constitutionality, and I think it is highly relevant to proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Professor, if you can look at this example which was raised in your report and confirm that this is an example of constitutional control over acts of the War Presidency even in the wartime.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally in order to preserve the legitimacy and legality of the system it was necessary for the constitutional court to function in wartime, too. And the constitutional court had its full composition throughout that period of time. So such a small body that has nine judges was able to function within an encircled Sarajevo, and this was of extreme importance for the legal nature of the system. And it was also extremely important for the laws of the highest body of power at that time be subject to the control of the constitutional court. I've mentioned the professional nature of the judges of the constitutional court and the ethnic composition of the bench, but I could also add that there were a series of other instructions, regulations, not only from the Presidency but from lower bodies of power. There were other laws that the court considered. When an Official Gazette published such regulations, these regulations wouldn't be valid if the constitutional court could suggest certain temporary proposals. And within a six-month time frame, they could order the person issuing the act, the law, to amend the law so that it was brought into line with the constitution. But at this point when this decree ceased to be applied - I think this is very important because the constitutional court ensures that the Presidency doesn't violate the basic democratic principles on the independence of the judiciary, and the independence of the judiciary naturally also involves the appointment of judges and relieving them of their duties. So there must be a clear and transparent system which makes it possible to check the moral and professional qualifications of the judges when they are being appointment. And the reasons for which they are being relieved of their duty before their office has expired. The Presidency probably had reasons to proceed without checking why certain individuals were relieved of their duties before their term of office had expired. I think this is of extreme importance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. This completes my re-examination

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise to the Chamber for having wasted time when looking for a document that I had before me. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does Mr. Kubura's Defence team have any questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I have a few questions I would like to put to you about your expert report and the numerous answers you have provided to the questions put to you by Defence counsel and the Prosecution. I will address the issue that was raised by the Defence just a minute ago. This concerns controlling the constitutionality of decree laws. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said the constitutional court would verify the constitutional nature of decree laws, but how would the constitutional court be seized of such a case? Who would refer such matters to the constitutional court?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina - and this is the case in other constitutional courts throughout the world - it is quite precisely stated which bodies can institute proceedings before the constitutional court. Usually there's a distinction made between an initiative taken and a proposal. If we have a system such as the system that existed in the former Yugoslavia, then the constitutional court could assess initiatives. And if they found sufficient grounds, they could institute proceedings before the constitutional court on its own initiative ex officio. But according to the rules, such proposals, and it depended on the law in question and on the laws that were violated, according to the rules the highest bodies of state authority, the members of the Presidency, the president, leaders in parliament, et cetera, had authority to act. And in the former Yugoslavia, this was also applied in that constitutional court, companies whose interests have been violated were also able to submit proposals to the court. This even included citizens, if their interests had been directly violated, infringed by the law in question. I would have to have a look at the decision, but in the decision, at the beginning of the decision, in the introduction, the person who has instituted the proceedings is always referred too. But it could have been the constitutional court itself if an initiative was submitted to the constitutional court. But the judges certainly know that in theory this is a very debatable matter. It's debatable as to whether the court itself should be granted the power to initiate proceedings because this perhaps conflicts with the principle of independence of the judiciary, independence of the court. We know there are certain systems according to which ex officio proceedings can be instituted, and as far as I know, in most systems the court remains absolutely neutral. But if we examined this decision, it quite clearly states who instituted proceedings to assess whether a given law, given decree, was in line with the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to your information in 1992, 1993, and 1994, how many times did the constitutional court have to deal with decree laws and render invalid certain decree laws? Could you provide us with an approximative number of the -- of how frequently the court had matters to referred to it and how frequently it had to render decisions on such matters.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the Chamber insists on this, it's quite easy to check the number because all the decisions of the constitutional court would be published in the Official Gazette. And in the yearly register for each year of the Official Gazette it states quite clearly how many such decisions were rendered. So it's very easy to obtain that information naturally. I don't have that information right now, but I mentioned something else in my report. For example, in one case the constitutional Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. court didn't render a decision but it had the authority, according to the constitution - and that's the case for many constitutional courts throughout the world - it had the authority to monitor phenomena that were of interest to ensure that the constitution was respected. And, if necessary, they could inform the relevant organs of issues in which the constitution was in question. In one case, there were rules that were to be established and published in an Official Gazette. Given the encirclement of Sarajevo, given the difficulty to obtain paper or to obtain equipment, et cetera, it quite frequently occurred that the Official Gazette was late in arriving in the field. But what was worse is that sometimes the number and the date of the Official Gazette would be far earlier than the date at which it was possible for this law to be passed. So sometimes it was necessary to apply some sort of rules retroactively, and that's not permissible, of course. And then the constitutional court provided information to the assembly and the Presidency and draw their attention to these circumstances. The court insisted on ensuring that the date for publishing material was respected, and it was also necessary to give those who had to be informed of the contents of the law to be informed in time. So this was an assessment of the constitutional court provided in an official letter which has been attached to the material here. This was also one of the ways in which the constitutional court drew attention to the fact that certain phenomena were not in accordance with the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this information. I would like to address the issue of the expanded Presidency. You said yesterday at the very beginning of the afternoon that the Presidency in peacetime was usually composed of seven members. But given the declaration of war, the Presidency was enlarged, was expanded. Could you tell me who in addition to the seven individuals composed the enlarged Presidency? Who were the three additional members who formed this Presidency?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since that is a very clear constitutional decree, this happened automatically. When an imminent threat of war was declared, and given the clear provisions of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then naturally the president who would schedule the first session of the Presidency would then have to call on those who according to the constitution were to become members of the Presidency. They were then supposed to be provided with some sort of a formal document showing that an imminent threat of war had been declared and that according to the constitution the president of the assembly, the prime minister, and the commander of the Territorial Defence staff would automatically become members of the Presidency. And it's necessary to point out that they were equal to the other members of the Presidency. Therefore, it was just as important as the vote of those who had been elected as members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Within the framework of the Presidency which was initially composed of seven members, two Croats, two Serbs, two Muslims, and one member who had declared himself to belong to the category of others, within that framework wasn't there a rotating Presidency that depended on the ethnic affiliation of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're quite correct. That collective head of state, according to the basic principle in force in the former Yugoslavia, there was a one-year term of office for the presiding member of the Presidency, but the presiding member was a primus inter pares, first among equals. He had protocol duties, he had to introduce the Presidency itself, sign the laws, schedule sessions, et cetera, et cetera. However, the constitution itself contained a provision which stipulated that if because of a state of war it was not possible to elect a new Presidency or if it was not possible to elect a president, then the existing composition of the Presidency would continue in the office until conditions for a new election were created and the president would continue in his term of office. Since the Presidency was elected in 1990, this situation occurred in 1994 because peacetime hadn't been achieved by that time. And after the signing of the Dayton Agreement in 1996 the first post-war elections were held and this was then in accordance with the Dayton constitution. A new Presidency was then elected which had three members, and the national and civic principles were combined. There were three representatives of the three constituent peoples, but all the citizens from entities would participate in the election, two from the federation, one from Republika Srpska. So this was a combination and not always a happy combination, a combination of the civic model. In part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, citizens would elect certain members of the Presidency, but there had to be Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You referred to the declaration of a state of war. Could you comment on item 3 in the declaration. We'll show the document to you. Mr. Registrar, could you show the witness P362 in the B/C/S version, which is the Official Gazette. We could perhaps place it on the ELMO so everyone can perhaps see the document. Could you please have a look at document 158, which should be on page 2 of the document. Number 158, document 158 is the declaration of a state of war. What I would like to know is the following: There's a statement of reasons for the declaration of a state of war. Could you comment on the reasons provided.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my report I already mentioned the reasons for declaring a state of war. This has to do with the fact that it was declared on the 20th of June, 1992, when the fighting escalated and in those first few days of the war, the number of civilian casualties was the highest. And the damage inflicted on towns and civilian buildings was extremely extensive. And the international community did not show that they had the will to put an end to that conflict, although there are a number of important documents from the international community which speak of the nature of the war and of the events taking place. I'd like to point out that there was a resolution of the Security Council dated the 15th of May, 1992, Number 752, and in this resolution it states that it has been determined in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina that regular forces of the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Croatia. And the Security Council explicitly requested that these forces withdraw from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina or that they place themselves under the command of the legal authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and naturally none of this was done. Given the way that events unfolded we know that sanctions were imposed on the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, and we know about everything that took place on the international scene. But as far as internal relations are concerned it became necessary to step up the level of organisation within the state and within the society in order to mount a defence. This decree law, or rather, this decision on declaring a state of war was then taken. And this puts into motion certain mechanisms that are necessary to protect the state. And naturally, a number of other measures were also taken, measures that are necessary to take, for example, declaring an all-out mobilisation. And I'd also like to point out, and this is something that we discussed yesterday, too, it's necessary to establish a political platform and to emphasise the values supported by the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina and emphasise reasons for which it was necessary to engage all patriotic forces and to engage them in the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And when the fighting was at its most intense, the Presidency still wanted a peaceful solution to the conflict, and they insisted on international negotiations to achieve such a solution. Everything was done to find a peaceful solution to the crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like you to comment on Article litem 5, paragraph 5, that there was a meeting held on the 20th of June, 1992. This session, was it a session of the Presidency or of the parliament? It is something I am unable to distinguish. The text was adopted by the Presidency or by the parliament or the assembly? The reference refers to whom exactly?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no doubt that it was a meeting of the Presidency, the enlarged Presidency, because the most intensive war operations, as far as I know from my personal experience, the most offensive operations occurred at the very beginning. For example, the very fact that I could not return to the country after going to attend negotiations in Brussels about the succession of states, and many other things confirm that this was a situation when there was absolutely no possibility for the assembly to meet. Therefore, this decision, quite legitimately, was adopted by the enlarged Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please look at point 3 when the state of war was declared for the whole territory, point 2 and point 3. How in legal terms do you interpret this point 3 regarding the devolution of the powers of the Presidency to the army. Because yesterday you told us the army was under the total control of civilian authorities, that is the Presidency. How can we link that to point 3 in this document? Could you comment, please, on the fact that it is indicated here that the army is authorised to take all necessary measures. Could this be considered as legal devolution of certain powers of the Presidency to the army and what is the ultimate controlling element?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. I think that the Presidency here is performing the function of civilian control. And according to the vertical system of command, it commands its units to take all measures necessary to protect the country from the war. My opinion is quite the opposite, that this point actually confirms that there was civilian control over the armed forces, because it was not the armed forces that decided to re-align themselves during a state of war, but it was the Presidency who took this decision, which was a civilian organ which had under its jurisdiction the armed forces, that is the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At this point in time, it was still the Territorial Defence and the beginnings of the formation of the army. So there were certain difficulties to carry out the transition from the Territorial Defence to the army because the Territorial Defence was inherited from the former Yugoslavia and then we started to develop our own concept of defence for Bosnia and Herzegovina. So my answer is quite clear: That this is a document indicating civilian command and political control over the armed forces, because from your question one could describe this as an example of self-restriction of one's own competencies, because after all the subsequent events confirm this because the Presidency as the supreme command continued to issue various by-laws and documents and decisions that confirmed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification. So you're telling us that the measures taken by the army were certainly under the control of the civilian authority, in this case the enlarged Presidency. Just before the break I would have a final question to put to you which is of a constitutional nature. According to the constitution in force at the time there was equality between the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. And in view of this equality, constitutional equality, was it possible within a unit of the 3rd Corps to call a unit a Muslim brigade? Is this name in your view constitutionally permissible, in view of the fact that in the constitution there was no distinction because everybody was treated on an equal footing? In your view the fact that there was a unit with an ethnic attribute, would that be constitutionally possible?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you that the constitution clearly stipulated the equality of all three nations and the rights of members of other ethnic groups. I'm not familiar with the concrete circumstances as to how this Muslim brigade came to be formed, but I could agree with you that it did not reflect the spirit of the constitution generally and it may have been questionable. But it is my impression, though I don't have any arguments for this, that this was more of a limited attempt because I don't know that there were many such units. But of course the military people know this better than I. And especially within the structure of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina there were no Serb, Croatian, or Muslim entities. As far as I know, this was quite an isolated case and it may have been a reaction to the existence of the Army of Republika Srpska, as they were officially called, or the Croatian Defence Council because both those components contained these national attributes. I agree with you that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was working to achieve the goals of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina in accordance with the constitutional principles, this was not quite in line with those principles. Now, how that actually happened, I don't have any detailed information, but I know there were a relatively isolated number of such units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is half past 12.00. We will have a break and we will resume about five to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I just have a few more questions before giving the floor to both parties. Just before the break I asked you about the 7th Muslim Brigade. A historical expert witness who came several weeks ago told us that in history there were cases when there were formations of units with the Muslim attribute. Are you aware of this? And he said that this 7th Muslim Brigade was just a continuation of something that existed before.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really not a historian and I have not studied history so much. But as far as I know during the Second World War there was one such brigade, but I really don't have any more detailed information. I do know, for instance, that some books have been written when Bosnia and Herzegovina was part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire there was a brigade of Bosniaks, and there is a book entitled, "The Bosniaks are Coming." But I don't think then it was used as an ethnic designation but rather people coming from Bosnia as Austro-Hungary treated Bosnia as a separate entity, but I couldn't give you any more information about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. My very last question. You told us yesterday that in November 1993 you were the Minister of Justice.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The functioning of the Ministry of Justice in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, did it mean that the minister had civilian prosecutors whom he could instruct to conduct Prosecutions?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Minister of Justice was a civilian and the prosecution is part of the judicial system and the judicial system is separate from the executive, so the minister is part of the executive. And the prosecutor's office is separate from the administration. Maybe as a citizen if I were if I were no give an initiative to the prosecutor, he may review it. But officially as a Minister of Justice I did not have any such experience, though I held that position for a brief period from November 1993 until August 1994. And even during that period I would be outside Bosnia and Herzegovina because of my obligations within the negotiations of a peace settlement. But I know that the Minister of Justice cannot give instructions to the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday you indicated with respect to questions relating to offences committed by servicemen and civilians, you said when the military prosecutor finds that he is not competent, he has to proceed, or at least that was my understanding but could you specify, that he needs to forward the file then to the civil prosecutor. Is that how you would explain a case when a file is incorrectly addressed to the military prosecutor, whereas in reality he has no jurisdiction. Could you tell us in view of the important positions that you held how at the procedural level, though I know you're not a specialist in criminal procedure but you told us that constitutional law does cover a very broad area, how is the situation resolved when the military prosecutor is not competent? As far as you know, what are the possible solutions?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to bear in mind two facts in this connection, first that this is a body that is absolutely competent to judge whether there are grounds for criminal prosecution; and secondly, a procedural principle is applied, and that is that throughout the proceedings one has to take into consideration the real and territorial jurisdiction of the deciding institution. In this institution, the military prosecutor is obviously competent to assess whether a criminal offence has been committed and it is his duty to watch over real and territorial jurisdiction. If he finds that there are elements for a criminal offence and that the military court is not competent, then he will forward this to the civilian prosecutor, otherwise it would not be processed at all, an act for which there are grounds to suspect that it does constitute a criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Following the questions that I have asked, do the parties as part of the adversarial system have any questions to put to the witness for further clarifications? I'm asking Madam Henry-Benjamin first whether he wishes to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has one question. Further cross-examination by Ms. Henry-Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor Trnka, can you clarify for the benefit of the Trial Chamber and for our own benefit as to at the outset of war, did the commander of the army replace the position of commander in the Territorial Defence in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In accordance with the transformation of the Territorial Defence into regular armed forces, that is the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is the key element of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this was a process. It was not something that happened in a single day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, that will be all, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Further examination by Mr. Bourgon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Welcome back, Professor. I just have a few questions arising from the questions by the Trial Chamber. The first being in relation to a question put to you by the Presiding Judge concerning the approximate number of times that the constitutional court intervened in the period 1992/1993. Your answer to this question was that this information would be published in the Official Gazette. I have here the Official Gazette which I would like to show to you with the consent of my colleague so you can maybe provide the Trial Chamber with this information and of course by putting the Official Gazette under the ELMO so that everyone may see. I am referring specifically to the Official Gazette of 1992, page 15. My colleague has informed me it is not -- it is within the Official Gazette but it is the register, or "le registre" [phoen].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To obtain more precise information on the number of times that constitutional court intervened with regard to rules and instructions issued by the authorities, I refer to the register which at the end of every year is attached to the Official Gazette. There is a register of all such matters and then usually put together in one category the laws of the Presidency, of the government, of the constitutional court, et cetera. Here under the laws of the constitutional court you can see how many such decisions were taken by the constitutional court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that the ELMO is not working properly. I am trying to see the text on my monitor. I don't know if the Chamber has it before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If everyone else can follow, Mr. President, it is not a problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Professor, I do not have what is displayed by the ELMO, but if you may continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I can say is that -- all I can mention is the number of decisions rendered by the constitutional. Now it would be necessary to carefully examine which decisions have to do with controlling constitutionality and which decisions deal with other issues for which the constitutional court has jurisdiction, but I don't think I could provide you with an answer by simply examining this document briefly. It would be necessary to examine it at length. I suggest the Defence proceed in this manner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I understand that it may not be possible for you to provide detailed explanations in this regard. But can you, based on the document you have in front of you, establish how many decisions were rendered by the constitutional court in 1992?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just go through this? I'll take it off the ELMO for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, it seems that in the B/C/S document the date at which cases were referred to the constitutional court were 1989, 1990, and 1991, and this does not relate to the question I wanted asked. Because I wanted to know whether during 1992, 1993 -- I wanted to know how many decisions had been rendered during that period, during the period 1992 and 1993, whereas this document seems to be referring to 1989, 1990, and 1991, but perhaps they are the relevant pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps I'll leave this aside and provide the Chamber with this information in the near future.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see 14 decisions that were rendered in 1992, 14 decisions rendered by the constitutional court. One should carefully determine the period that the decisions referred to, but this is a technical detail. And naturally 1993 is relevant here because Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. according to the rules of procedure for the constitutional court, what -- the cases examined in 1992 were probably examined in 1993, too. So it would be necessary to have a look at the register from the Official Gazette of 1993 and 1994, because some cases that had been commenced in 1993 would have final decisions in 1994. So if we had such elements at our disposal, we could obtain very precise information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you very much, Professor. I will move on to my next question arising also from a question put to you by the Presiding Judge concerning the enlarged Presidency. You confirmed that the three additional members on the enlarged Presidency consisted of the prime minister, the commander of the Territorial Defence, as well as the president of the assembly. Now, my question to you is: We see that one of these three members happens to be a military officer. Can you confirm that at the district level and the municipal level there were no army members as part of the enlarged Presidency? And to be more specific, that the commander of the municipal defence staff was not on the municipal Presidency and that the commander of the Territorial Defence staff was not on the district Presidency.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But to be sure we are quite clear, we have to make a clear distinction between the position of the enlarged Presidencies and the composition of the municipality Presidencies and district Presidencies. They have no particular authority. They only operate as municipal assemblies or rather as district assemblies, and their power is limited to decisions of those bodies. I must make another distinction. According to the system that existed up until the time when the state of war was declared, or rather up until the time when a law on defence was issued, according to the old system that prevailed in the former Yugoslavia the commander of the Territorial Defence in the municipality was envisaged as a member of the Presidency. But since Bosnia and Herzegovina did not automatically adopt the rules about these subjects from the former Yugoslavia, it started organising itself in a different way immediately. I remember that immediately after an imminent threat of war had been declared, the republican Territorial Defence staff was declared as the staff of Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign state. It was no longer something that existed within some sort of Yugoslav system, the Yugoslav state. And then the commander of the staff was no longer a member of the Presidency. But this perhaps relates to what we're discussing. In the Presidency there was a secretary for defence which would be analogous to the Minister of Defence at the level of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But since the secretary only had military civilian authority and not military authority, it means that in a certain sense a clear distinction was made between civilian and military structures. These two spheres were clearly delineated. So in municipalities and districts, according to the rules of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina staff, there weren't staff commanders of municipalities and districts, not in the Presidencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. My next question relates to the proclamation of the state of war which was raised with you by the Presiding Judge, and my question here is quite simple. I would just like to confirm that when we see the mention of armed forces, what exactly are we talking about in addition to the army and what is a distinction between the two terms?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Put very simply, armed forces are all the legitimate formations and armed individuals in the state who were part of the structure of power and who at some point in time, when an imminent threat of war is declared or a state of war is declared, engaged in defence. You quite rightly pointed out that this was above all the army. That was the only defensive force in peacetime, but in wartime, in addition to the armed forces the police are engaged, some of the customs officers who carry weapons are engaged, and even people from the security forces of various companies can legally carry weapons. Since they're all armed and within the system, they are all part of the armed forces, and this is a subject we have discussed on a number of occasions, both today and yesterday. And I said that the relation towards the police and the army members was different. It depended on how the chain of command worked in both cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, just as a follow-up question to your response. In the documents that you have used in making your report you referred to a number of decree laws. Can you help us with the distinction in general terms between the decree law on defence, the decree law on the armed forces, and the decree law on service in the armed forces. Is there a relationship between these three decree laws, and what did they refer to in general terms in order to allow us to better understand the situation?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally there is an organic relation, but if we have a look at the time when these decrees were issued we can see that they followed on each other. One could say that first general ones were issued and then more specific ones. The decree law on defence deals with the potential of a society that must be employed for the purposes of defence. This does not only refer to armed possibilities, but also the tasks of the civilian authorities and to the overall organisation at all levels of power in order to mount a defence. This is a general global or overall approach to ensure that the state and society can mount a defence in such exceptional circumstances. Naturally the civilian organs and the military organs have different tasks. So there is within this system of defence an armed forces system. And we try to make a further distinction within the idea of armed forces. There's the position of the army, the position of the police, and a fairly marginal role played by other armed elements, customs officials, border officials, et cetera, et cetera. We can then make further distinctions, and there are regulations on internal order within the army. These govern the relations between the soldier and an officer, the rules of service, et cetera, et cetera. So one's going from general principles down towards more specific principles. And finally, we have instructions that stipulate how soldiers should behave, officers, units, et cetera, et cetera. So they have material and a temporal and a logical connection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. My last question deals with the issue that was raised by the Presiding Judge in respect to equality of all three nations, and this is a topic which is covered in your report. I would simply ask: Can you confirm that the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was a multi-ethnic army even though it was comprised of less Croats and less Serbs because most of these had left to join either the HVO or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have a look at the structure of the military formations in the ABiH, as I have said, it was exceptional to appoint only people or to employ people from just one nation, and given the general formation of military units, for example, a mountain brigade, this company, that company, in all these cases you don't have such an attribute, no national attributes. So as you have just said in your question, given the information we have on the composition of commands, at the very top of the command there are Croats and Bosniaks. I can confirm that in the international negotiations we were accompanied by a Croatian officer. In the corps command, there was Mr. Jovan Divjak, a Serb. And there's a number of other cases I could mention. If you have a look at the composition of the command of units, I'm sure that the statistics could be checked and the information would confirm that the army had in its ranks members of other ethnic groups. But the policies pursued by the civilian organs were such that they insisted on the multi-national composition, and these are the values that Bosnia and Herzegovina is based on. And in the introduction to my report, and I think it's also relevant for peace plans and for the subject that we are discussing, in the introduction I said that there was certain things that were constant in the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in Bosnia and Herzegovina today. That was a state in which there were various religions, cultures, customs, and within that context a tradition of mutual tolerance and respect had been developed. And from a legal point of view, in my opinion, this was of extreme importance. And I have referred to this on a number of occasions in some of my papers. And the internal territorial organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, either when it was independent or either when it was part of the Ottoman or Austro-Hungarian Empire or when it was part of the former Yugoslavia, the kingdom of Yugoslavia from 1918 up until 1941 and especially after the Second World War, the internal administrative organisation within Bosnia and Herzegovina was never based on a national principle. Unfortunately, and I can say this from my own point of view, this principle was only advocated in the peace plans of Bosnia and Herzegovina; that's when they first started advocating this principle. And yesterday I referred to the Stoltenberg Plan, and the Dayton Agreement isn't against establishing such a certain national structure either. So certain imbalances formed in terms of the nationality of people. This isn't the best basis upon which Bosnia and Herzegovina would develop as a civic society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask the other Defence team whether they have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Trnka, this concludes your examination. You have spent two days here to answer the questions put to you by Defence counsel, the Prosecution, and by myself. Thank you for your contribution that you have been able to make, given your knowledge of constitutional matters and your knowledge of other things as well. We appreciate all the answers you've provided to all the questions and we thank you. I wish you on behalf of the Trial Chamber all the best and a safe trip home and naturally I also wish you all the best when pursuing your career in the field of constitutional matters. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would first like to thank you. The Defence called me here and the Trial Chamber showed interest in my report. I would also like to thank the Prosecution. If I have contributed to clarifying certain subjects, I'm extremely glad to have been of help. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the documents that are going to be tendered are concerned, there's certainly a long list of them, would it perhaps be better to establish a list and disclose it to the Defence [sic] and in the course of another hearing we could deal with the issue. If there are only a few such documents we could deal with them rapidly. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe with the Chamber that it would be better to wait so I can disclose a list to the Prosecution, and then they can check that the documents in the report are the ones that they have been provided with and that they can be admitted into evidence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And similarly the documents that you mentioned yesterday, some of which haven't been translated, perhaps by that time you'll have the translation of these documents. We'll see about that at a subsequent date. We have another five minutes. Are there any issues you would like to raise? As far as the schedule for tomorrow is concerned, I'll give the floor to the Defence. Do you want to go into private session now? Shall we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher, thank you for bringing the binders. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there anything Mr. Bourgon would like to say? Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to inform the Chamber that we received the military expert's report yesterday morning. We have -- we'll start checking the footnotes this afternoon and the report should be disclosed to the Prosecution by tomorrow morning. This will help us to plan the end of the Defence case for General Hadzihasanovic. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, the Prosecution will have 30 days, but perhaps they won't need this time. So we will wait to hear what their position is. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As we have indicated previously, we will endeavour to review that report as quickly as possible. And as I asked my learned colleagues yesterday if they could forward us electronically a copy of that report, that would expedite our review of it as soon as they have reached the conclusion that it's ready for filing. If we could have that electronically as well, that will at least save us one day of it going through the registry, and we can also work much quicker with an electronic copy. So we will do our best, Mr. President, and hopefully in the next day or so we will be meeting with both Defence teams to talk about some planning and expediting the proceedings in order to bring the trial to a close as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that information. It's 1.45, and I will see everyone at the hearing that is to be held on Thursday at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
